Hi, my friend! I’m glad you found your way to my website!
I’m Siyu Chen, an undergraduate student in Psychology， currently working in the Meta-Self Lab under the supervision of Hu Chuan-Peng. My interests mainly focus on Artificial Intelligence for Psychology during this phase. Specifically, I’m doing some research explorations of Computational Modeling based on Artificial Neural Networks, to train a model behaving like a human (which is super fun, isn’t it?), trying to uncover the cognitive mechanism of decision-making processes. Besides, I’m also fond of music and shooting photos, fascinated by philosophy, and have passion for exploring the ground truth of this world. Exercising like boxing, climbing and running are in my daily life as well.
I try to do research in a way that is transparent, reproducible, and inclusive. This may include things like publishing preprints, sharing data and code, and contributing to open source software development.
Feel free to take a look around and contact me if you have any thoughts or find any errors, hopefully we can make something great together!

title: Research Projects
text:
Ongoing Projects


Visual Evidence and Decision Dynamics in Human Reaction Time
Ongoing 2025 - Present
Description: This project develops a computational framework linking visual evidence, conflict effects, and recurrent decision dynamics to explain human reaction-time patterns. Using the flanker task as a test case, the current work examines how age-related differences, stimulus-driven uncertainty, and time-varying evidence shape response speed and accuracy. The present model shows promising progress in capturing key behavioral structure, while ongoing work continues to refine the mechanism and improve its fit to full human data.
My Role:

Designing and implementing hierarchical neural-network models for reaction-time behavior
Building analysis pipelines to compare model behavior with human flanker-task data across age groups
Interpreting internal model dynamics to study how visual evidence and conflict unfold over time

Methods & Tools Used:

Python (PyTorch)
Convolutional Neural Networks
Recurrent Decision Dynamics
Computational Modeling
Behavioral Data Analysis

Outcomes:

A mechanism-oriented model that reproduces several core reaction-time distribution patterns and guides ongoing model refinement

Collaborators:

PI: Hu Chuan-Peng, School of Psychology, Nanjing Normal University




Completed Projects


RNN Modeling and Neural Dynamics in the Face-Switch Task
Completed 2026 Apr - Jun
Description: This project investigated monkey neural population activity in a face-switch task to understand how neural representations support flexible decision-making. The analyses focused on population-state geometry, task arrangement, and choice-related dynamics, with the goal of clarifying whether switching behavior reflects stable representational structure, dynamic reconfiguration, or both. The project combined data analysis and RNN-oriented modeling to examine mechanism-level constraints on flexible decisions rather than static representations alone.
My Role:

Analyzing neural population data from a face-switch decision-making task
Developing workflows to study trajectory geometry, switching-related structure, and choice dynamics
Integrating PCA, linear decoding, and FINDR-style modeling to interpret recurrent neural dynamics

Methods & Tools Used:

Python
Principal Component Analysis
Linear Decoding and Classification
FINDR-Style Modeling
Neural Population Dynamics Analysis

Outcomes:

Produced structured analysis reports, reusable figure-generation workflows, and a consolidated result package for studying neural dynamics and flexibility in the face-switch task

Collaborators:

Gouki Okazawa, Institute of Neuroscience, Center for Excellence in Brain Science and Intelligence Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences



A Cognitive Mechanism Exploring of Fast-Same Effect
Completed 2024 - 2026
Description: This project built a neural network model incorporating cognitive processes to simulate the fast-same effect in matching tasks and explore its underlying cognitive mechanisms. The fast-same effect refers to the phenomenon in which participants respond faster to “same” trials than to “different” trials. By developing an artificial neural network model grounded in decision-making processes, the project aimed to better understand the mechanisms driving this effect.
My Role:

Designing and implementing neural network architectures for simulating the fast-same effect
Training and validating models against human behavioral data from matching tasks
Analyzing model performance and interpreting results to uncover cognitive mechanisms

Methods & Tools Used:

Python (PyTorch)
Artificial Neural Networks
Evidence Accumulation Models
Computational Modeling
Behavioral Data Analysis

Outcomes:

Resulting paper currently in preparation

Collaborators:

PI: Hu Chuan-Peng, School of Psychology, Nanjing Normal University




Research Interests


I am broadly interested in:

Cognitive Computational Modeling: Developing computational models to understand decision-making, learning, and related cognitive processes.
Artificial Neural Networks: Using neural network approaches to study human behavior and neural data, especially in perceptual and speeded decision tasks.
Perceptual Decision-Making: Investigating how sensory evidence, uncertainty, and prior structure shape behavior over time.
Open Science: Supporting transparent, reproducible, and accessible research through open data, open materials, and open-source tools.
